A safety test was conducted to determine how far a motorcycle takes to stop when traveling at different speeds. The test was conducted in winter, and the results are shown in the quadratic model plotted above.

  1. [MATH: 95]

  2. [MATH: 120]

  3. [MATH: 130]

  4. [MATH: 105]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/182ca7910f88613f7dc6ff632d52acde]

A safety test was conducted to determine how far a motorcycle takes to stop when traveling at different speeds. The test was conducted in winter, and the results are shown in the quadratic model plotted above.

According to the model, which of the following is the best estimate for the stopping distance, in feet, if the motorcycle was traveling [MATH: 35\,\textrm{mph}?]

1. [MATH: 95]
2. [MATH: 120]
3. [MATH: 130]
4. [MATH: 105]

sections.normalized_html:
From the graph, we note the following:

  • At [MATH: 30 \, \text{mph},] the stopping distance is about [MATH: 85 \, \text{ft},] and

  • At [MATH: 40 \, \text{mph},] the stopping distance is about [MATH: 130 \, \text{ft}.]

Since [MATH: 35\,\text{mph}] is a value between [MATH: 30\,\text{mph}] and [MATH: 40 \, \text{mph},] we can estimate the stopping distance by finding the mean of the corresponding distances for these two speeds: [MATH: \frac{85\, \text{ft} + 130\, \text{ft}}{2} = 107.5\, \text{ft}]

Therefore, among the choices, the closest estimate for the stopping distance at [MATH: 35 \text{ mph}] is about [MATH: 105 \,\text{ft}.]

Since [MATH: 35\,\text{mph}] is a value between [MATH: 30\,\text{mph}] and [MATH: 40 \, \text{mph},] we can estimate the stopping distance by finding the mean of the corresponding distances for these two speeds:

Therefore, among the choices, the closest estimate for the stopping distance at [MATH: 35 \text{ mph}] is about [MATH: 105 \,\text{ft}.]
